screens.body:
A wireframe is a skeleton sketch of a screen: boxes where things go, labels for what they are, zero styling. No colors, no fonts, no real text — just structure. "Header here, task list here, big Post button here."

Why so ugly on purpose? Because polish invites comments on polish. Show a rough sketch and people critique the LAYOUT — which is exactly what you're trying to get right first.

options: A rough structural sketch of a screen — boxes and labels, no styling
check.question: A wireframe is…

screens.heading: Skeletons before skin
screens.keyPoint: Ugly on purpose: critique the structure, not the style.

screens.body:
Prototypes come in three fidelities — how "real" they feel. Lo-fi: paper sketches or grey boxes, clickable if you're fancy. Mid-fi: digital, realistic layout, fake data. Hi-fi: looks and behaves like the real app, with real content and interactions.

Start lo-fi and climb only when the questions change. Lo-fi answers "is this the right flow?" Hi-fi answers "does this feel right?" Building hi-fi too early means polishing a flow you might throw away.

options: Lo-fi (rough) → mid-fi (realistic layout) → hi-fi (like the real app)
check.question: Prototype fidelity levels:

screens.heading: Lo-fi to hi-fi
screens.keyPoint: Climb fidelity only when the questions change.

screens.body:
Each fidelity level has CONSTRAINTS — things you deliberately DON'T do yet. Lo-fi: no colors, no real text, no pixel-perfect alignment. Mid-fi: no final branding, no complex animations.

Constraints aren't laziness; they're focus. Every hour spent picking button colors on a lo-fi wireframe is an hour stolen from testing whether the flow makes sense. Decide the constraints up front and defend them.

options: Deliberate limits per level (e.g. no colors in lo-fi) that keep focus on the right questions
Rules about what users can do
check.question: Constraints in prototyping are…

screens.heading: Rules for each level

screens.body:
Interfaces are built from a small set of elements: buttons, text inputs, dropdowns, toggles, cards, navigation bars, modals. Learn the standard ones and their expected behavior — users arrive with habits from a thousand other apps.

Formatting matters too: align things, group related items, give elements room to breathe. A screen where everything screams for attention is a screen where nothing gets it. Hierarchy — what to look at first, second, third — is doing half your communicating for you.

options: Standard elements (buttons, inputs, nav) arranged with clear visual hierarchy
As many different widgets as possible
check.question: Interface building blocks:

screens.heading: The pieces on screen

screens.body:
Color guides attention: the brightest, boldest color should mark the most important action — everything else quiets down. And contrast — the difference between text and background — decides whether people can actually READ your interface.

This is also accessibility, not decoration. Low-contrast grey text on white might look sleek, but it's unreadable for many users — including anyone in bright sunlight. Standards exist for minimum contrast ratios; meeting them isn't optional polish, it's respect.

options: Color directs attention; strong contrast keeps text readable for everyone
Low contrast looks premium so it's fine
check.question: Color and contrast:

screens.heading: Color with a job
screens.keyPoint: Brightest color = most important action; contrast = readability.

screens.body:
A prototype is a FAKE version built to answer questions — "would users find the post button?" — without building the real thing. Paper, clickable mockups, even role-played flows all count.

The magic word is throwaway. Prototypes are meant to be wrong fast and discarded. If you're polishing a prototype, you've missed the point — it's a question-asking machine, not a product.

options: A fake version built to test ideas cheaply — meant to be thrown away
check.question: A prototype is…

screens.heading: Fake it before you make it

screens.body:
Iterative design is the loop: sketch → test with users → learn → refine → repeat. Each round answers the current questions and raises better ones. You converge on good instead of gambling on perfect.

Three rounds of rough-and-tested beats one round of polished-and-hoped. Every iteration is cheap because the prototype is cheap — that's the whole economic argument for this entire topic.

options: Sketch → test → learn → refine, converging through cheap rounds
check.question: Iterative design means…

screens.heading: Round and round, getting better
screens.keyPoint: Converge through cheap rounds, not one big gamble.

screens.body: W3C Web Accessibility Initiative (w3.org/WAI) — official contrast and accessibility standards. Material Design (material.io) — Google's official component and color guidance. Nielsen Norman Group (nngroup.com) — research on prototyping methods and fidelity.
screens.heading: Go deeper
screens.keyPoint: WAI sets the official accessibility bar.
